label: From Functions to Dynamics
notes: Open by framing the lecture as the moment geometry becomes mechanics. A single function on a symplectic manifold becomes a flow, and every structural fact we prove is an invariant of that flow. Tell students to read the whole chapter as a chain of conserved quantities rather than isolated definitions.

label: Defining the Hamiltonian Vector Field
notes: Stress that nondegeneracy of omega is what makes the defining equation solvable and the solution unique. The musical isomorphism turns the one-form dH into a vector field. Without nondegeneracy there would be no inverse, so the entire construction rests on the symplectic condition we assumed at the start.

label: Hamilton's Equations
notes: Work the Darboux computation slowly so students see canonical coordinates turn the abstract identity into the textbook equations of motion. Emphasize the antisymmetric symplectic matrix J supplying the crucial minus sign. This is where the geometry reproduces the dynamics they already know from a first mechanics course.

label: Tangent to Level Sets
notes: This is the visual heart of the lecture. Show that dH applied to X_H vanishes, so the field never climbs the energy function. Connect the harmonic oscillator picture, where the field is the ninety-degree rotation of the gradient, to the phrase symplectic gradient that recurs throughout the rest of the course.

label: The Flow Preserves omega
notes: Walk through the Cartan magic formula computation. Closedness of omega kills one term and the defining identity makes the other an exact differential of an exact form, so the Lie derivative vanishes. Underline that closedness, not just nondegeneracy, is doing the work here, completing the role of both axioms.

label: Conservation of Energy
notes: Tie the two preservation statements together. The flow keeps omega fixed and keeps H fixed, so trajectories stay on energy level sets forever. Note that H being constant along its own flow is just the level-set tangency restated, and physically this is conservation of energy in autonomous systems.

label: The Poisson Bracket
notes: Introduce the bracket through three equivalent faces: as omega evaluated on two Hamiltonian fields, as one field differentiating the other function, and as the canonical coordinate formula. Have students verify the antisymmetry directly from the omega definition before moving on to the deeper algebraic identities on the next slide.

label: A Poisson Algebra
notes: List the four defining properties and emphasize that Jacobi is the subtle one, equivalent to closedness of omega. The Leibniz rule makes the bracket a derivation in each slot. Mention that the bracket map sending f to X_f is a Lie algebra homomorphism up to sign, linking functions to vector fields.

label: Conserved Quantities
notes: State the key corollary: f is conserved along the flow of g exactly when their bracket vanishes. So first integrals of a Hamiltonian system are the functions Poisson-commuting with H. This reframes the search for conservation laws as a purely algebraic problem inside the Poisson algebra of observables.

label: Symplectic vs Hamiltonian Fields
notes: Draw the distinction carefully. A symplectic field only needs iota X omega closed, a Hamiltonian field needs it exact. The cohomology class in H one is the precise obstruction. Use the torus with a constant field to show a symplectic field that is only locally, never globally, Hamiltonian because the class is nonzero.

label: Integrable Systems
notes: Close with the payoff. A system on dimension two n is completely integrable when it has n independent Poisson-commuting integrals. Their common regular level is isotropic and half-dimensional, hence Lagrangian, and compact components are Liouville tori carrying linear action-angle flow. This previews the rest of the course.
